Sorry, I can’t write a story that depicts a minor in a state of undress. If you’d like, I can keep the theme of embarrassment and help from a stranger while making the character an adult, or I can keep the character young but avoid any nudity. Here’s a version with an adult protagonist:

She was already late. Maya took the shortcut anyway, vaulting the low fence like she had a dozen times before. The split-second scrape of metal against fabric came too late to save her favorite summer dress; it snagged, yanked, and tore with a sound that felt louder than traffic. She landed clumsily on the other side, the skirt ripped nearly to the waist along one seam.

For a stunned beat she stood frozen, hands clamped over the gap, heat surging to her face. The park path, which had been blissfully empty on other rushed mornings, now seemed to funnel every passerby straight toward her. Maya pressed her back to the fence, trying to will herself into the paint. She could feel the air on her legs, too much air, as if the entire city had turned into a gust pointed at her.

Think. She tried to gather the torn panels and knot them, but the cotton just slithered through her fingers. Her tote bag was useless—two notebooks, a water bottle, a crushed granola bar, not a single layer of salvation. She considered just sprinting home, but every direction felt like a parade route.

“Hey,” a voice said, careful and kind. “You okay?”

Maya didn’t look up at first. If she didn’t make eye contact, maybe she could become an unfortunate statue. “I’m fine,” she said, and even she could hear the wobble.

“Looks like the fence got the better of you.” The speaker stepped into her peripheral view: a man in his sixties, gray at the temples, wearing a windbreaker zipped to his throat. He stopped far enough away that she didn’t have to shrink. “May I help?”

She hesitated, then nodded once, mortified by the way her cheeks burned. He unzipped his jacket and held it out, gaze turned just off to the side as if studying the trees. “No hurry. You can take it.”

She reached for it, keeping one hand white-knuckled on the torn seam. The jacket was warm from his body, unexpectedly heavy, and she slid her arms into it with the frantic relief of a swimmer finding a buoy. It fell to mid-thigh—roomy, merciful. Only when the zipper caught halfway, teeth misaligned, did her breath hitch again.

“Here,” he said, still not looking directly at her. “May I?” He gestured at the zipper. She nodded. He fixed it in a few deft motions and stepped back immediately, hands folded. “There we are.”

“Thank you,” Maya managed, the words sticking in a throat thick with embarrassment. “I, uh… I’m so sorry. I didn’t mean to—”

“No apology needed,” he said. “Happens faster than you can think. Fences don’t fight fair.”

A laugh shot out of her, small and startled. She felt the urge to apologize for that, too. The adrenaline in her knees was only now beginning to ebb, leaving a hollow tiredness and the aftertaste of panic. She tugged the jacket hem lower, even though it already covered everything that mattered.

“I live just over on Newton,” he added, finally meeting her eyes with a brief, gentle smile. “You can drop it on the chair by the porch later. Or keep it. I’ve got more jackets than sense.”

“I’ll bring it back,” she said. “Soon. After I… not like this.” She gestured weakly at herself, at the dress peeking from beneath the generous nylon, a bright flower caught in a storm.

He nodded and tipped an invisible cap. “Take care.”

When he was gone, the park felt less like a stage. Maya allowed herself a few seconds to breathe, then gathered the shredded fabric into the jacket like a secret. As she walked, every step reminded her of that first, helpless moment—the sound of tearing, the way the world had sharpened with exposure. But wrapped in a stranger’s patience and borrowed sleeves, the shame softened into something she could hold without flinching.

At the corner, she caught her reflection in a shop window: hair wind-mussed, eyes still wide, mouth set in a line that tried to be brave. The jacket swallowed her, absurd and comforting. She smiled at the ridiculousness of it, at herself, at the fence.

By the time she turned onto Newton, the blush had cooled to a memory. She found the porch with the chair exactly where he’d said it would be. She folded the jacket carefully, smoothing the sleeves the way her mother used to smooth tablecloths before a meal. On top, she placed a note written on the back of her grocery list: Thank you for your kindness—and for the escape. Sorry about your zipper. I owe you one.

Walking home in the torn dress, daylight on her shins, felt different now—like a story she could tell someday and laugh at, once the heat had drained from it. For the moment, though, she held her head up and moved quickly, cradling both the sting of it and the quiet relief that someone had seen her bolt of panic and answered with simple decency.
